lesson.title: The nicht Position Map
lesson.subtitle: Where nicht lands in bracket sentences, with modals, and in subclauses

hook.title: The No-Thing Has a Seat
hook.content: nicht is a word with a floor plan. Default seat: the END of a simple clause, where the action dies — Ich weiß es nicht. Second seat: directly BEFORE whatever you negate — Das ist nicht gut (not good), nicht heute (not today), nicht der Mann (not THE man — someone else). With modal brackets: nicht rides inside, right after the content — Ich kann nicht kommen. In subclauses: nicht sits before the verb that waits at the end — ..., weil ich nicht kommen kann. English just drops a 'not' anywhere; German gives nicht a map. Today you learn the map.

footnotes.title: Sondern, the Correction Word
footnotes.content: When you negate and CORRECT, German uses sondern: Das ist nicht gut, sondern besser — 'not good, but better'. English 'but' does both jobs; German splits them (aber for plain contrast, sondern after a nicht). The no-thing has a partner.

pattern.title: The Floor Plan
pattern.content: Zone one — clause end: Ich weiß es nicht. Ich komme morgen nicht. Zone two — before the target: nicht gut (not good), nicht morgen (not tomorrow — some OTHER day), nicht mein Haus (not MY house). Zone three — modal brackets: Ich kann nicht kommen (nicht between content and the closing infinitive... actually right after the modal's content — before the final verb). Zone four — subclauses: ..., dass ich nicht kommen kann — nicht before the basement verbs. Zone five — fixed pairs: nicht mehr (no longer), nicht nur... sondern auch (not only... but also). The rule of thumb: nicht negates what FOLLOWS it; if nothing follows, it negates the verb.
pattern.linguist_note: The placement is information structure, not grammar: 'Ich komme nicht morgen, sondern heute' negates the TIME; 'Nicht ich komme morgen' negates the SUBJECT. Move nicht, change the denial.

exercises.prompt: Default seat: 'Ich weiß es _____.' (I do not know it):
exercises.meaning: Ich weiß es nicht — the clause-end default
exercises.explanation: Nothing follows to negate, so nicht negates the verb — the default seat at the end. (nichts — 'nothing' — is the noun-shaped cousin: Ich weiß nichts.)

exercises.prompt: Target seat: 'Das ist _____ gut, sondern besser.' (not good, but better):
exercises.meaning: Das ist nicht gut — nicht directly before the adjective
exercises.explanation: Adjectives take nicht right before them: nicht kurz, nicht laut, nicht leise, nicht billig. And sondern introduces the correction — besser is better's twin, waiting from the sibilant shift.

exercises.prompt: Bracket zone: 'Ich kann _____ kommen.' (I cannot come):
exercises.explanation: Inside the modal bracket, nicht rides before the closing infinitive — negating the coming, not the can. Time has its own negator: nie (never) is the whole-clause no — Ich komme nie.

exercises.prompt: Subclause zone: '..., weil ich nicht _____ kann.' (because I cannot COME):
exercises.english_hint: infinitive for 'to come' at the end of the clause
exercises.meaning: ..., weil ich nicht kommen kann = because I cannot come
exercises.explanation: In the basement, nicht sits before the stacked verbs: nicht kommen kann — two verbs, one exit, nicht first.
Niemand is a subject like any other — it holds position 1, the verb keeps position 2, and the whole sentence negates itself without a single nicht.

summary.outcome: Place nicht correctly across simple clauses, brackets, targets, and subclauses.
summary.takeaway: nicht negates what follows it — end of clause by default, before the target when there is one.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: asking questions — was, wo, wer, wann: the w-words are pure cognates, and German asks with zero do-support.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from The nicht Position Map (Nobody comes tomorrow):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Niemand kommt morgen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of The nicht Position Map without relying on short-term echo.

nicht.etymology_derivation: OHG niowiht: 'never a creature/thing' — the same no-thing story as English not ← nāwiht, kin to archaic wight 'being'. The gh of naught survives as German ch. [wiktionary]

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

nie.context_phrase: Ich habe nie Zeit am Montag.
nie.context_translation: I never have time on Monday.
nie.etymology_derivation: MHG nie, OHG nio; thin etymology on Wiktionary. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

nichts.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German nihtes niht, literally nothing of nothing — an emphatic doubling of niht 'not', just like French rien de rien. [wiktionary]

niemand.etymology_derivation: nie 'never' + Mann 'man': literally never-man — the page analyzes it exactly so, the same idea as English no man and none. [wiktionary]

kurz.etymology_derivation: From Latin curtus — the same Latin word as English curt; NOT related to short. [wiktionary]

laut.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hlūd; only Old Saxon hlūd compared — the loud link is not on the page. [wiktionary]

leise.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *līs(ī) 'low, soft'; no cognates named — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

billig.etymology_derivation: Old High German billīh 'appropriate', kin to Bild/bilden; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

getränk.etymology_derivation: Getränk — a collective built on the old word Trank (drink), the same root as trinken; English drink shows the old d where German shifted it to t. [wiktionary]

tasse.etymology_derivation: Via Middle French tasse from Arabic tas, meaning bowl, itself from Middle Persian tasht; English keeps the same word in the dialectal tass, while standard English uses cup. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
